en: Oṃ, homage to the Omniscient One!

Having realized the ultimate truth, he who was Śvetaketu in Tuṣita for the sake of the people there became Śākyaketu here in this world for the sake of the living beings; may he, who has conquered death and displayed infinite skillful means, be victorious! 1.1.

Having bowed with reverence to the Fully Awakened One— who has attained the state of being free from old age and death, who brings about that state of freedom from old age and death, and who exists for the sake of attaining that very state— VMv_1.2.

It is said that what is consistent with the scriptures is difficult for those of dull intellect to understand, difficult for those of wavering minds to practice, and is a deceptive snare of death. (VMv 1.3)
In every respect, deception regarding death is appropriate only for those who are liberated; for all those who are not liberated, it is merely a delay for some time. (VMv 1.4)
The cessation of life-force, the faculties, and consciousness is the characteristic of death;
prolonging life through skillful means is called the deception of death. (VMv 1.5)
As long as one who practices the Dharma with senses subdued remains in saṃsāra, for that long they produce the equipment of merit and so forth that accomplishes awakening. (VMv 1.6)
Nothing substantial whatsoever is seen in cyclic existence apart from life;
therefore, one should swiftly begin to deceive death by various means. (VMv 1.7)
Nothing is difficult when applied through skillful means joined with logic;
for the power of jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs is universally acknowledged.
Having recognized death from afar by its signs, one should apply the appropriate remedy;
for what can even a person of great wisdom do when the thunderbolt-fire falls upon his head?
The characteristic of death is described as being twofold, through the distinction between external and internal; by means of this, those who are diligent may know that death is imminent.
If anyone should desire to know the signs of death, they must do so while their body is healthy; otherwise, there will be doubt.
Because of an imbalance of the elements, due to disease, through the influence of cataracts and the like, or by the power of fear, grief, and so forth, [an object] appears otherwise. (VMv 1.12)

Having encountered death characterized by three types— disturbances caused by fate, spirits, or both— one should therefore examine the arising of the fatal signs (ariṣṭa) according to their specific distinctions.

Disturbance caused by fate is considered to be of two kinds, through the distinction between external and internal; one should likewise determine that disturbance caused by spirits is also twofold. VMv 1.14.
Death resulting from the agitation of divine forces is called *ādhidaivika* (supernatural).
The agitation of divine forces is characterized by such things as fasting to death and the falling of thunderbolts.
Death resulting from the agitation of the elements is called *ādhibhautika* (pertaining to other beings);
however, the agitation of the elements consists of disturbances such as bile and other humors, or fire, water, and so forth. (VMv 1.16)
Death arising from the agitation of both is said to be born of both;
the agitation of both consists of afflictions such as wind, bile, and phlegm, and so forth. (VMv 1.17)
Because the omens are infinite in number, their simultaneous arising is not admitted;
nor do they all arise sequentially, but rather by numbers such as one and so forth.
Where death is observed in some cases despite the absence of [visible] signs, the fault lies there with the person attempting to determine it, and not with the non-existence of the signs. (VMv 1.19)
Even when a characteristic is observed where death is nowhere to be seen, one who is free from delusion should not postulate other obstructors of dharma and so forth in that case. (VMv 1.20)
When death is certain and far off, one should strive for great renown by acting according to one's ability through both renunciation and remedial measures.
Having become constantly composed, with a mind one-pointedly directed toward that, one should first observe the external characteristics. (VMv 1.22)
The time for discerning the characteristics is held to be twofold; it should be understood with effort as being both determinate and indeterminate. (VMv 1.23)
It is said that at the time of the sun's transit, the full moon, and so forth, the specific moment consisting of dawn and the like is fixed; however, the opposite case is unfixed.
The cheeks may throb at the joints excessively due to the sight of death, as well as from contact with wind, cold, and so forth; therefore, these signs should be distinguished from one another.
The zodiac sign Cancer corresponds to the month of Āṣāḍha, while Capricorn is considered to correspond to Puṣya;
furthermore, the signs of Cancer and Capricorn are characterized by death.
On the day of the Āṣāḍha-saṃkrānti, at midday,
the shadow of one standing facing north shall be naturally equal to the length of a single foot.
On the day of the sun's entry into the constellation Puṣya, that very same [measurement] shall consist of seven steps;
and at midday in a cloudless sky, there is the observation of the shadow.
If there is an increase of syllables month by month, or a decrease of syllables month by month,
or if it becomes otherwise than this, a suspicion of death arises.
There is an increase of one pada each from Āṣāḍha until the end of Makara;
there is a decrease of one pada each from Makara until the end of Karkaṭa.
From Āṣāḍha there is a gradual increase [of the shadow], and likewise from Puṣya there is a gradual decrease;
having observed this change in the shadow, one should predict death according to the months.
If there should be an increase during the time of decline, or a decline during the time of increase,
then starting from that very moment, death is certain within a month.
Even during the period of increase, if there is excessive increase, there will be affliction from various diseases;
even during the period of decrease, if there is excessive decrease, death itself will occur without a doubt. (VMv 1.33)
At the end of Āṣāḍha and Puṣya, and previously at the beginnings of Karkaṭa and Mīna, there are six days each; herein lies the determination of the proper and improper times.
By means of these remaining days of Āṣāḍha, one determines the auspicious and inauspicious [outcomes] at the beginning of Śrāvaṇa;
and by means of the remaining days of Puṣya, one determines the auspicious and inauspicious [outcomes] at the beginning of Māgha and so forth. VMv 1.35.
When, having pierced the *tālukā* of the two feet, a piercing occurs at the navel, then after three days and nights, death ensues. (VMv 1.36)
If, having pierced the sole of the feet, one also pierces the eyes,
then after three months there will be a journey to the abode of Yama.
If, having pierced the *tālukā* of the feet, one then pierces the nose, then indeed within three days that person goes alone to the state of the five elements. VMv 1.38.
If the *hañchikā* [pulse] is equal in both the hut and the urinal at the same time, then indeed death will come to him within that very year. (VMv 1.39)
If the piercing of the nasal bridge occurs, death will happen in five years;
if the tip of the tongue is no longer visible, men shall die in three days.
Death will occur after four months from a sharp piercing at the tip of the ear;
death will certainly be instantaneous from piercing the location of the *ūrṇā* (the hair-tuft between the eyebrows).
When the piercing occurs simultaneously for both the moon and the sun, then death shall occur after one month; therefore, one should accumulate merit.

If, during the union of the bhaga and liṅga, there is a *hañchikā* in the middle and at the end that is equal [in intensity], then one goes to the state of the five elements (death) within five months. (VMv 1.43)
He whose four joints— the two of the hands, the two of the feet, and the two of the little fingers— are pierced simultaneously within a month, is destined for death.
When the piercing sensation occurs simultaneously at the centers of the heart and the throat,
death will occur within three fortnights, provided one does not practice the Dharma.
If one should repeatedly pierce the three palates simultaneously,
then death will occur within three days, even if one were equal to Śakra himself.
He who does not see the reflection of the shadow of his own left eye in a mirror will surely die within seven days, unless there be a remedial treatment.
If, during sexual intercourse, the sound of a bell should reach the ears,
then death will occur within three months, even if one were equal to Brahmā himself.
If what was black becomes white on the first lunar day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight, death will occur after six months; if it is red, it indicates disease.
If piercing occurs separately at the root of the ear, between the eyebrows, or on the crown of the head,
and it cannot be remedied, then death will occur instantly.
If the piercing, accompanied by a burning sensation, extends from the big toe up to the navel,
that person will certainly die within six months.
From the big toe up to the heart, or to the throat, or to the head—death occurs respectively after three months, three fortnights, or one day. (VMv 1.52)
Due to the loosening of the flesh at the tip of the nose, death shall occur after seven nights;
due to the severing of the flesh of the cheeks, death shall occur after five months.
If no throbbing is perceived between the eyes and the nose, one should know that death will occur within five days and gather a store of merit. (VMv 1.54)
If the pupils of the two eyes suddenly become blurred,
death will occur within six months unless remedial measures are taken.
If the nose suddenly becomes crooked, the ears fall from their natural positions, and the eyes become round, death will be seen within seven days. (VMv 1.56)
If the heart suddenly sinks, then death will occur within a fortnight;
likewise, from the severing of the two channels situated at the sides of the neck, death occurs within a fortnight.
If a black line suddenly appears in the middle of the tongue,
or if there is a firm clenching of the teeth, then death will occur after two nights.
From observing the severance of the channel on the back of the ear-cavity,
death occurs on that very day or within five days.
If, when the nails are red in color, they suddenly become colorless,
then death will occur within six months, unless one practices mantra and other such remedies.
If one suddenly becomes stout, thin, angry, or overwhelmed by fear,
his death will occur within a year, provided he does not practice the Dharma.
When the sense faculties no longer grasp their respective objects, when speech falters repeatedly, and when there is frequent confusion of the mind; VMv 1.62.
His eyes constantly discharge fluid, and he experiences confusion even when seeing forms; furthermore, he does not perceive his own reflection in a mirror or in water. (VMv 1.63)
One may see a rainbow at night, or a circle of stars during the day; one may see lightning flashing toward the south in a cloudless sky. (VMv 1.64)
During the day, one may see the path of a shadow, as well as the falling of a meteor;
or one may see swans, crows, and peacocks gathered together in one place. VMv_1.65 //
One may see two moons or two suns, as well as one's own head ablaze, or a city of Gandharvas atop a tree or on a mountain peak. (VMv 1.66)
He may see hungry ghosts, piśācas, and other invisible, terrifying beings;
he trembles violently and may repeatedly fall into a swoon. VMv 1.67.
If one should see vomit, urine, and feces each appearing with the luster of gold and silver, his death shall occur within the limit of one month.
If one should see cuts or holes on the throat, lips, palate, tongue, or likewise upon the body, death will certainly occur within six months for that person.
If one's throat, lips, palate, tongue, and teeth dry up individually and repeatedly for six months, one should predict his death.
The non-appearance of the circle of constellations, the Seven Sages, and the cardinal directions at night,
as well as a sudden flame appearing on the body, portends death within seven days.
If one suddenly fails to see Arundhatī, Rohiṇī, Dhruva, and the Chāyāpatha during the night, one should predict death within six months.
The moon free from stain, the sun devoid of rays, the fire-god Citrabhānu together with his rays, and the moon also together with its rays. VMv_1.73 //
Seeing the sun at night and the moon by day, as well as fire in one's own eyes,
a star the size of Mount Meru, and the ocean like a river— VMv_1.74.
Hiccups at the navel, pain in the anus, a lotus-like complexion on the face, red pustules on the throat, and a variegated coloration of the limbs. (VMv 1.75)
In the heart, there is weeping with tears and trembling;
then, at the palate, the moonbeam feels like the touch of fire, and the sunbeam feels cold as snow.
He who perceives the aperture of the moon, the aperture of the sun, as well as the aperture on the earth and likewise in the sky, by means of his own self, shall see death within a fortnight.
If urine, semen, and feces fall simultaneously, death will occur within a year; in such a case, medical treatment and other remedies should be applied.
If one half of his body is cold and likewise the other half is hot, death will occur within seven nights; he should then contemplate the next world.
The sound *ha* has a cold touch, while the sound *pha* is like fire;
for one who experiences these, the vision of Yama occurs within ten days.
If a black line is seen at the bases of the ring fingers,
death will occur eighteen days hence due to the fault of past karma.
If a three-colored chameleon climbs onto one's head and moves about with speed,
death for that person is certain within five months.
If no sound is heard from the body when it is rubbed with both hands,
then due to the coldness of all its limbs, death is certain within ten days.
If, while walking, the emergence [of breath] from both the arms and the shanks occurs simultaneously, there is a rupture of the *brahmasūtra*; for such a person, death will come within one year.
If a footprint appears broken, with a deficiency either in the front or the back, in mud or on dusty ground, death will occur within four months.
If one suddenly sees a man of dark-brown complexion,
death will occur after the passing of three years, provided it was not imagined through delusion.
If, immediately upon bathing, the heart and feet dry up, death will occur in two months;
if a foul odor arises and the appearance becomes distorted, death will occur in three nights.
On a day when the sun is in its harsh [southern] course, one should fill the cavity of the mouth with water;
blowing forcefully every day, one should gradually [expel it] situated within that [cavity].
A long-lived person may always see the variegated rainbow;
however, one whose life lasts but six months shall not see it—such is the diversity of karma.
On a Sunday, one should look ahead toward the center of the sky at those adorned with pearl ornaments, appearing like strings of pearls that have been severed.
Having the hue of sapphire gems and the appearance of a mass of hair,
they move away from the visible location and spread toward another place.
One should see numerous nāgas constantly as if they were restrained;
if they are not seen for six months, death is proclaimed. (VMv 1.92)
At dawn or at evening, or for a long time before the moonlight,
one should extend the arms forward and, having seen one's own clear shadow, gradually look toward the sky.
Even there, a white shadow in human form may be seen;
because his head is not visible in it, his death shall occur within a year.
From the non-appearance of the left hand, there will be the destruction of one's sons and wife;
from the appearance of the right, [there is the destruction] of one's father, brothers, and other great elders.
Placing his arms above his knees and likewise joining his palms at the crown of his head,
he should observe the shadow resembling a plantain fruit situated between the two.
But when a single petal there is observed to be blossomed,
then certainly death shall occur within six months on that very lunar day.
When the vital wind has entered the path of the sun, these three signs are to be observed:
sound in the ears, smoke in the head, and likewise light in the eyes.
Covering the ears very firmly, a deep, gurgling sound is heard for five days, ten, or fifteen days. (VMv 1.99)
Death occurs, respectively, after twenty days, or twenty-five, or five hundred and forty, or one thousand eight hundred years.
Within these intervals as well, sixteen days are to be subtracted,
by means of one-fourth parts of the year itself, increased sequentially.
If one does not see a wreath of smoke emerging from above the head for seven days, death shall occur for that person within a limit of three years.
By pressing upon one's own eyes with the fingers, lights resembling the eyes of a cat appear instantly in the four directions. (VMv 1.103)
Even if there is no affliction, death shall occur within a hundred days upon seeing that [sign].
This should be understood as the general rule; however, the specific detail is now stated.
Likewise, if the light [of the breath] disappears below the moon, above it, at the ears, the nose,
or the vicinity of the temples, death shall occur after six, three, two, or one month respectively.
If the movement of the moon were also toward the sun as before,
then death would occur on the days numbered by the directions (ten), arrows (five), qualities (three), and eyes (two).
Due to the reversal of one's own form, death will occur in six months;
death will occur in five months from the destruction of the tip of the nose.
If deafness occurs in the two ears, death will occur after the passing of four months;
if there is a falling out of a healthy sense organ, death will occur after three months.
If light is not seen between the eyebrows, the vision of Yama occurs within two months;
after the lapse of one month, death follows from the wasting away of the testicles.
If the reflection in one's own eyes is not seen, death occurs within seven days;
if the tongue does not turn back, there is an encounter with death after ten days.
If [the breath] reverses at the navel, death will approach within five days;
however, if it is drawn toward both sides, death shall occur after three days.
If there is stiffness of all the limbs, death will occur after one day;
from the disappearance of the three lines on the forehead, death occurs after three days.
If the tongue of a healthy person is devoid of saliva, lacks tactile sensation, and is free from moisture,
death will occur within five days, or likewise after fifty days.
Acidity in taste and blueness in color,
as well as a morbid change in semen and urine, indicate the sight of death within six months.
If one's urine should flow simultaneously in five streams, or if it swirls counter-clockwise and lacks its natural odor, his death will occur within six months.
Whether in the dark fortnight or the bright fortnight, if the semen is extremely black,
death will occur within six months unless there is a remedial treatment by that very means.
Having abandoned the dark portion and taken hold of the bright portion,
when the moon is blowing [toward] the east wind, there shall be a remedy through entry.
"Even if one's own body is stable, if its shadow is flickering, those expert in the scriptures say that death will occur after four months. (VMv 1.118)
If one sees the shadow of oneself cast toward the southern direction, one should contemplate impermanence, thinking: "Death will come for us this very day. (VMv 1.119)
Because it is revealed that [a dream] is meaningless, deceptive, false, and so forth, even a dream is unreal for everyone; therefore, it is not appropriate to place trust in it.
Furthermore, that man for whom a dream shown by a deity is a true dream,
having gained confidence from that dream, should observe the signs of death.
He who climbs a *kiṃśuka*, a *kovidāra*, or a flowering *karavīra* tree at the end of a dream will die within six months.
The person who, at the end of a dream,
climbs a monastery pillar or a heap of sand or ashes, will meet death as previously described.
Just as one who has mounted a donkey and travels toward the southern direction might never return, such is his life as well. (VMv 1.124)
Furthermore, if one who has mounted a monkey should set out toward the southern direction,
and while staying there he should perceive [the omen], his death would occur as before.
Any man who climbs upon a staff, a sacrificial pillar,
an anthill, or a heap of dust, shall not live for six months.
That wrathful Kālī Kumārī who binds with fetters should be known as Kālarātrī; she brings about death within seven days.
But that woman who wears black garments and desires a man,
and who in her dream wears a garland of oleander flowers, goes to the realm of Yama.
If one enters darkness in a dream, or likewise a chasm or a prison;
or if one falls from a tree in a dream, such a person stands in the presence of death.
He who sees a tree, grass, or wood as fruitless—whether asleep on his head or on his body—does not live for six months. (VMv 1.130)
If a man mounted on a monkey-chariot should travel toward the eastern direction, one who has awakened should know: "This is my final night. (VMv 1.131)
He is devoured and even dragged away by dogs, crows, vultures, jackals, rākṣasas, pretas, and piśācas; and by donkeys, pigs, camels, and cattle.
One should certainly predict his death at the end of one year;
as for the signs seen in dreams, the pacification [of their effects] is a wisdom that is like an illusion.
Having seen before him a black man holding an iron staff and dressed in black attire, one meets death after three months.
His limbs smeared with red ointment, adorned with red garlands,
anointed with oil, extremely terrified, shaven-headed, and clad in red garments.
If one sees oneself in a dream mounting a donkey and traveling with speed toward the southern direction, such a person has six months to live.
Whoever receives red garlands, perfumes, or even red garments in a dream, for that person death shall occur within eight months.
The external signs of death are beyond numbering; who is able to describe them with a single voice, even in hundreds of years?
Having recognized these external signs of death as they have been described, one must swiftly apply effort toward their evasion through mantras and other such means. (VMv 1.139)
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśa* (Instruction on Deceiving Death) composed by the venerable scholar Vāgīśvarakīrti.
Now the internal signs of death are clearly described;
they are to be known through the arising of the vital winds, for the wind is the domain of the nose and the mouth. (VMv 2.1)
A correct determination regarding death cannot be made based solely on external signs, as long as the internal signs have not been correctly ascertained. (VMv 2.2)
From the certainty regarding both, death would clearly be certain;
externally, there is a perversion of cognition even toward conditioned things such as disease and the like.
During the solar transits (saṃkrānti) of the months beginning with Puṣya, and on festival days such as the full moon,
one should observe the general characteristics of death starting from the morning.
On whichever day the person who determines the time should determine the time [of death],
starting from that day, death will occur upon the expiration of the limited period.
For all living beings whose constitutions are balanced,
[the breath] always rests individually in the right and the other nostril.
The wind flows for half a watch during the periods known as the Sun and the Moon;
from the reversal of this, death and other events should be inferred by the wise.
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, the wind flows through the moon for three days; thereafter, it flows through the sun for three days.
Again, for three days in the moon [phase], and then for three days in the sun;
by this sequence, according to the rule, until the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight.
In this manner, when the wind blows in the sun starting from the dark fortnight,
it continues for three days as before, until the fifteenth day of the other [fortnight].
If this sequence is reversed, death will occur within six months once the three positions have been thoroughly ascertained; therefore, one should then attend solely to the Dharma. (VMv 2.11)
From the reversal of both sides, there will be calamity for friends and kinsmen;
from the reversal of one side, the occurrence of a terrible disease arises. (VMv 2.12)
If the wind should flow for one, two, three, four, five, or six days in reverse order, then distress, agitation, and so forth arise.
The vital wind (vāyu) may flow through all three paths due to the complete avoidance of its natural course;
after midday, death occurs, devoid of any remedy.
If for ten days the wind flows through both pathways without any transference [of breath], he indeed dies at the time of the transference.
If one's eyes throb at the moment of the equinox, one should know that his destruction will occur within a day and night; of this there is no doubt.
If the wind should blow in many directions here and there for half a watch, one should know that for that person there will be honor and indeed gain. (VMv 2.17)
If the wind should flow through the mouth after bypassing the five points of transition (*saṃkrānti*), for that person there will be loss of wealth, or agitation, or fear and the like. (VMv 2.18)
If the wind flows through the left nostril after passing thirteen transits (saṃkrāntis), disease and other afflictions arise for that person. VMv 2.19.
When [the breath] departs through the mouth, having abandoned the two nostrils,
that is the end of his life, even if he were as firm as a diamond.
If the wind blows toward the sun for five days starting from the time of the transit [of the sun] into Mārgaśīrṣa, death occurs after eighteen years.
If the wind should blow for five days starting from the time of the solar transit (saṃkrānti) in the month of Aśvayuja, death shall occur after fifteen years.
If death occurs in Śrāvaṇa in this manner, it will happen within twelve years;
if it should likewise occur in Jyeṣṭha, death would take place within nine years.
If the wind should blow for five days starting from the time of the sun's transition into the month of Caitra, then death will occur after six years.
If the wind blows for five days following the solar transit (saṃkrānti) of the month of Māgha,
those skilled in the knowledge of time declare that death will occur after the passing of three years.
If the wind should blow for two, three, or four days in every [sign],
those portions of the year must be subtracted accordingly and in proper sequence.

In the same way, if the wind flows in the lunar channel, one is freed from death; likewise, diseases, famine, wilderness perils, grief, and afflictions such as those caused by kings and the like [will cease].
This clear general understanding of time has been demonstrated;
now another method is shown for the sake of understanding specific time.
If the Moon is in the birth asterism when the Sun has reached the seventh sign,
that time is known as Pauṣṇa, which brings about the determination of death.
Whichever other sign is the seventh from the zodiacal sign in which a man was born is known as the "equal-seventh" (samasapta); in that [sign], the Sun is situated at the equal-seventh.
If the Moon should be in that very same zodiacal sign as the birth asterism, it should be known as the Pauṣṇa time; therein lies the determination of death.
The wise man should determine the time when [the sun] is everywhere within its course and moving constantly; at any other time, it is an improper hour.
At whichever tide-mark the movement of the wind proceeds differently, when that tide-mark is reached, there is death; of this there is no doubt.
If, during the period of Pūṣan, the wind flows for half a day in the direction of the sun,
then one should recognize death after a number of years equal to that of Manu (fourteen).

If [the breath] flows for one day, a full day and night, two days, three days, four days, seven days, ten days, seven mountains (seven), six, and four Vedas (four) years respectively, death occurs in those respective times.
If [the breath] flows for five days, ten days, or likewise fifteen days for three, two, or one year respectively, death will occur accordingly. (VMv 2.36)
If the wind should blow in that very same manner for twenty or twenty-five [days],
death shall occur after six months and three months respectively.
If [the breath] flows for six, seven, eight, twenty-eight, twenty-nine, or thirty days less [than a month],
death occurs respectively after two months, one month, a fortnight, ten days, and five days.
If [the breath] lasts for thirty, thirty-one, or thirty-two days, then death will occur after five, three, or two days respectively. (VMv 2.39)
If the wind blows toward the sun for as long as thirty-three days, on that very day death occurs even for Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
Regarding those sixteen days that are not mentioned among the intervals between the fifth and twenty-fifth days, their purification is now described.
If [the breath] lasts for six days, [death occurs] after three years minus twenty-four;
if for seven days, after three years minus twice the previously stated amount.
If it lasts eight days, [death occurs] after three years minus seventy-two days;
if it lasts nine days, [death occurs] after three years minus ninety-six days.
If the wind, moving within the solar sphere, blows for eleven days,
death will occur within twenty-four nights, or rather, within two years.
For twelve days [one should practice] two years prior to the previously mentioned [period], reduced by double that amount;
for thirteen days two years after [that], reduced by seventy-two days.
For one who is two years old, [the period] is fourteen days less ninety-six days;
for one who is one year old, it is twelve days less, [calculated] by a cycle of sixteen-day periods.
If the wind moves solely within the domain of the sun for seventeen days,
death is declared to occur within twenty-four days less a year.
Eighteen days less than one year and thirty-six days; or, if it is nineteen years, less forty-eight days. (VMv 2.48)
Twenty-one [days] after six months less six days;
twenty-two [days] after six months less twelve days.
When the journey takes twenty-three days, it is [calculated] from [twenty-four days] minus eighteen days;
when the journey takes twenty-four days, it is [calculated] from [twenty-four days] minus six days.

Thus, the occurrence of the signs of death within exactly thirty-three days is to be understood as resulting from the force of the arising of the vital winds; it cannot happen beyond that point, as it is impossible.
And it is said here:

"Starting from half a day, then for the whole day, then for a full day and night, and then for two days, three days, and extending up to four days—when the breath residing in the channel flows during the rising of the Sun (the right side), this should be known as the auspiciousness of the six, four, worlds, sun, and directions. (VMv 2.52)

From five [days], the progression here increases by five every twenty-five days; from that point, it increases by one more each time until it reaches thirty-three. During the period of Pauṣṇa, those months are thirty-three, six, twelve, and sixteen; those months are the days, while the remaining [days] of life are fifteen, ten, sixty, and twenty-two. VMv_2.53.
Having drawn a three-layered wheel provided with thirty-seven compartments,
one should write down the days of the lifespan and of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) according to the sequence of their numerical values.
Thus, I have also described these internal signs of death, which have another name, *ariṣṭa*.
Having recognized them, those who are swift must immediately apply effort toward the very evasion of death through meditation and other such means. (VMv 2.55)
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Instruction on Deceiving Death*, composed by the venerable scholar Vāgīśvarakīrti.
Having understood the collection of external and internal omens of death, one should also understand the accumulation of deceptions, both external and internal. VMv 3.1.
The external [is purified] by bodily and vocal actions, and the internal by the actions of meditative concentration;
the external [is purified] by jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs, and the internal by the powers of yoga.
Those who are intent on deceiving death can accomplish it through faith;
therefore, one should strengthen one's faith, for otherwise there would be nothing but great exhaustion. (VMv 3.3)
The subtle Dharma is not attained even by gods who lack faith, neither through various forms of bodily mortification nor through heaps of wealth. VMv 3.4.
Faith is the supreme, subtle Dharma; faith is knowledge, austerity, and the oblation;
faith is heaven and liberation; faith is this entire world.
Even if one were to give away all one's possessions and even one's very life without faith, one would not obtain any fruit at all; therefore, one should possess faith. VMv 3.6.
At the outset, one should be devoted to the Dharma out of a desire to deceive death;
for the Dharma protects from death, and death is deceived by the Dharma. (VMv 3.7)
One should not remain even for a single moment devoid of Dharma through negligence;
for even Brahmā is not a master over deceiving death without Dharma. (VMv 3.8)
For those who are esteemed by the wise— whose dharma consists of truth, generosity, austerity, and forbearance,
and especially compassion— what need have they for extensive discourses on dharma?
For those whose hearts are constantly overflowing with compassion toward sentient beings, they possess both wisdom and liberation; what need is there for any other extensive teachings on the Dharma?
Non-violence is the supreme dharma, agreed upon by all philosophical systems;
for one who constantly practices it, death gradually recedes to a distance.
Even one of short life may become long-lived immediately by reviving these—birds, fish, deer, beasts of prey, thieves, and others—who have arrived at the place of execution. (VMv 3.12)
Even one who is long-lived may become short-lived instantly by killing these beings—thieves, fish, deer, beasts of prey, and birds—who desire to live. (VMv 3.13)
By abandoning the ten unwholesome actions, by taking refuge in the Three Jewels,
and likewise by observing the five and eight precepts, death shall be kept at a distance.
Protecting those held in bondage, those afflicted by severe diseases, and those terrified by fear, he shall surely become long-lived and a deceiver of death. (VMv 3.15)
By respectfully bestowing desired objects upon the poor, the helpless, the modest, and those endowed with virtuous conduct, one's lifespan certainly increases. (VMv 3.16)
Through reverence for one's mother, father, teachers, elders, and those advanced in knowledge,
and by offering honor and hospitality, death does not approach at all.
By constantly and respectfully beholding and saluting one's own chosen deity, its devotees, and those bearing their sectarian marks in the morning, an increase in longevity is attained.
By providing bricks and other materials for a ruined or cracked stūpa and the like,
one who was short-lived may become very long-lived, as in the case of the mendicant who subsisted on alms-food.
Through the act of constructing monasteries, stūpas, images, and the like, by planting groves, and through the eight great modes of worship, one’s lifespan increases constantly. VMv 3.20.

By means of substances obtained through the alms-gathering of a *chandaka* monk, through feeding the Saṅgha, one’s lifespan will become long—even if it was originally limited to seven days—just like King Dharmāśoka. VMv 3.21.
By constructing a stūpa out of sand, likewise by striking a drum, and by venerating stūpas and the like, one’s lifespan certainly increases. (VMv 3.22)
The Mahāsamājaka Sūtra, as well as the Āṭānāṭīyaka, along with the Kṣudrakas, the Mahāmegha, and the verses known as the Susvasti. VMv 3.23.
One should cause the monks to recite it with due honor, or one should recite it oneself;
having thus attained long life, one becomes a deceiver of death. (VMv 3.24)
One who constantly recites with one-pointed concentration the sūtras such as the Gaṇḍavyūha, which illuminate the Mahāyāna, attains the deception of death.
By reciting all the Yoga Tantras and other scriptures spoken by the Buddha,
or through the ritual procedures of the *Pañcarakṣā*, the deception of death is attained.
By performing circumambulations of the Uṣṇīṣagarbha-caitya and other such shrines,
and by the recitation of dhāraṇīs, death is warded off by those who are diligent.
Through the recitation of the *Mātṛkā* beginning with the planets (*graha*), preceded by its prescribed ritual, and through the chanting of the *Ratnolkā-dhāraṇī* one thousand times; VMv 3.28.
The wise, devoted to the recitation of the *dhāraṇīs* prescribed in the *Dhāraṇīsaṃcaya* and other such texts, render even imminent death distant. (VMv 3.29)
Through the drawing of mandalas, through fire offerings, through the binding of mudrās,
and through the offering of bali-oblations and gaṇacakra feasts, there is the deception of death.

By giving food, bedding, and other necessities to the noble Saṅgha of the four quarters, or even to those who have merely the saffron robe around their necks, there may be the deception of death. (VMv 3.31)
From the undertaking of such actions as these, there arises merit characterized by virtue;
from merit comes the increase of lifespan, and through that increase, the deception of death.
Thus, the Dharma has been briefly indicated; its full detail should be inferred by those who would deceive death, having understood it for themselves. VMv 3.33.
Thus, being devoted to the Dharma, one should perform the warding off of death by means of perfected mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth, which produce immediate results.
By the power of jewels, mantras, medicinal herbs, and perfected elixirs, the defeat of death itself has been witnessed by the Siddhas and Vidyādharas, as if by their own hand.

One who holds the vajra having passed the examination prescribed in the treatises on the characteristics of jewels, or likewise one who wears a life-prolonging gem, or one who assumes a universal form; VMv_3.36.
One who wears a priceless sapphire or any other great gem will undoubtedly be a deceiver of all deaths. (VMv 3.37)
And in this matter, no doubt regarding the efficacy of the jewel is logical, because it is universally accepted that jewels possess inconceivable powers. (VMv 3.38)
Having performed worship before a cloth painting or similar object,
one who goes to a secluded place achieves the deception of death through the mere recitation of mantras.
One should first utter the syllable *ā*, and then clearly the syllable *ro liṅ*;
this is known as Trailokyavijaya, proclaimed in the Vidyādhara-piṭaka.
One who is endowed with faith should recite this mantra of Lokeśvara one hundred thousand times; before him, he will certainly attain the deception of death.
Having first recited Vairocana, one should subsequently utter Tāre twice, Tuttāre twice, and Ture twice, ending with Svāhā; this is the deception of death.
Having recited one hundred thousand syllables of the mantra taught in the *Tārābhyudaya-tantra* before Noble Tārā, preceded by offerings of curd and honey...
By performing oblations with dūrvā grass and young sprouts from the northeast peak,
one may ward off even death arising from the power of past karma.
Oṃ; first *ruru*, then *ataḥ*, then the word *sphuru*, followed by that;
then *jvala*, *tiṣṭha*, and likewise the three words *siddhalocane*. (VMv 3.45)
The mantra *sarvārthasādhani svāhā* should be written upon a stainless leaf of the *aśoka* tree by preceptors who have been given ritual fees, using liquid sandalwood. (VMv 3.46)
Whether by the hundreds of thousands or even by the tens of millions, one who is pure through the performance of faith—
having been washed with waterless milk— or having offered oblations of dūrvā grass and the like, [attains success].
He will certainly become one who effects the complete deception of death, and he also becomes one who brings about the pacification of the entire multitude of diseases. (VMv 3.48)
Of this mantra known as the Noble Hundred Syllables, whose inconceivable power is described in the *Mahāmaṇḍalakalpa* and whose efficacy has been witnessed many times over; VMv_3.49.
Through the method of undertaking the Bhadracaryā and reciting it one hundred thousand times, even liberation will surely be attained; how much more so the deception of death?
First, there should be "Homage to the Tathāgatas of the three times," and after that, the phrase "the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) which has attained unimpededness everywhere. VMv 3.51.
From the word *balinām*, [one recites] *oṃ*; then the word *asamasama*;
then the word *samantato 'nantatāvāptiśāsanī*. (VMv 3.52)
Hara hara! Smara smara! From the state free from passion, there arises the nature of the Buddha-dharma; then, sara sara, she becomes one of equal power. (VMv 3.53)
There should be two *hasa*s and two *traya*s, O Gaganamahāvara;
then, in the characteristic [mantra], there should be the word *jvala* followed by *jvalanasāgare*. VMv 3.54.
By adding the word *svāhā* at the end, it becomes the hundred-syllable mantra;
this is proclaimed as the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) of all the Tathāgatas. (VMv 3.55)

By reciting the mantra of the Noble Mahāpratisarā one hundred thousand times and performing a fire offering (homa) with dūrvā grass one-tenth that amount, the deception of death will certainly be achieved.
Oṃ, having uttered the words "pure," "victorious," "excellent," and "immortal," one should then immediately speak the words "hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. (VMv 3.57)
From Vairocana, one should utter "bha-ra" twice and "saṃ-bha-ra" twice;
having spoken the word "indriya-bala," one should recite the words for purification.
HŪṂ HŪṂ RURU CALE SVĀHĀ—this mantra is the deceiver of death;
it is the heart-essence of the Noble Mahāpratisarā, which bestows all accomplishments.
Having recited that ten-syllable mantra known as Mṛtyuñjaya one million times,
one should then perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with white flowers one hundred thousand times.
By offering one hundred thousand oblations soaked in ghee before the Teacher, the Lord of the World,
the power of the mantra will then inevitably bring about the deception of death.
Oṃ; first then the syllable Āṃ, after that the syllable Īṃ, Ūṃ, Oṃ, Mṛtyuñjaya, Oṃ—this mantra consists of ten syllables. (VMv 3.62)
The mantras taught by the Tathāgatas for the purpose of living for an eon and so forth have been used to achieve a long life; that long life is the deception of death. (VMv 3.63)
By those mantras through which rites of pacification are performed, there shall be an increase in lifespan;
by those through which there is an increase in lifespan, there shall be the deception of death.
Doubt regarding the efficacy of mantras is not at all consistent with reason,
since the inconceivable power of mantras is accepted by everyone.
And it is said:
"There is nothing else in the world that cannot be accomplished through mantras;
mantras are like wish-fulfilling gems when one applies oneself with right faith. (VMv 3.66)
Or else, according to the procedures taught in the Kalpa, or by practicing as one desires, one should employ *amṛtā* extensively in a region where hunger is prevalent. (VMv 3.67)
Whether taken alone or combined with other medicines,
it always renders the body firm, so that one no longer beholds the gateway of death.
By the use of other divine medicinal herbs as well, there is an increase in lifespan; through the destruction of old age and disease, one does not behold death.
From a corpse bound with space, gold, and so forth, and consumed according to the ritual procedure,
there shall be the evasion of death, due to its nature as a perfected elixir (*rasāyana*).
By means of the internal element obtained through the conjunction with the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight and other such times,
the deception of death occurs through the administration of nasal drops according to the prescribed rite.
Through the application of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) as taught in the Saṃpuṭa and other tantras,
when performed according to the instructions, the deception of death occurs.
For one who constantly practices the beneficial yoga of the "sealed union" (*saṃpuṭayoga*) by means of the upward and downward [breaths],
even King Yama— though enraged— cannot obstruct his splendor and will be unable to do him the slightest harm.
Even the restoration of the dead has been seen in some cases through a specific means:
by means of chains produced from a menstruating maiden and a man. (VMv 3.74)
By means of the bodily constituents known as semen mixed with blood, which are not excessively cold, or by drops of the constituent elements that have fallen from one who has just died; VMv_3.75.
Having introduced [the smoke] through the exit of a tube-hole smeared with ghee,
one should gradually inhale it into the nostril-cavity raised by one's own nose-tip.
The restoration of life is observed here, and cessation is likewise praised;
this yoga, whose efficacy is directly perceived, is highly esteemed by many. (VMv 3.77)

Alternatively, the yogi should constantly practice the fivefold nectar-elixir (pañcāmṛtarasāyana), either in its entirety or individually, combined with the three myrobalans (triphalā) and *mārkava*. VMv 3.78.
Free from wrinkles and grey hair, possessing a vajra-body and his own natural form, he will certainly ward off death even for the duration of many kalpas. (VMv 3.79)
This is established by scripture: for many people, through the consumption of water and the application of fragrance, there shall be the immediate warding off of death. (VMv 3.80)
And by the constant practice of these two, combined with honey and clarified butter,
one may ward off death, even that which has arisen out of season.
Even regarding the efficacy of medicine, doubt is certainly not appropriate, since the power of inconceivable herbs is observed everywhere. (VMv 3.82)

Having thus diligently performed the external rite for deceiving death here according to one's ability, now, out of fear of the powerful and great terror of death, perform that internal practice once again. VMv_3.83.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Instruction on Deceiving Death*, composed by the venerable scholar and master Vāgīśvarakīrti.
Now, however, the internal skill for deceiving death is being described, by which death is certainly deceived by those who apply themselves with diligence. (VMv 4.1)
Staying somewhere on a mountain or similar place—free from the fear of kings, thieves, pestilence, tigers, and the like, and secluded from worldly contact—it is delightful. (VMv 4.2)
Eating in moderation, speaking sparingly, not fond of excessive walking, sleeping little, meditating much, and being devoted to the recitation of mantras. (VMv 4.3)
One should be devoted to the practice of reciting the true Dharma, such as the worship of one's chosen deity,
and intent upon the offering of oblations at the three junctions of the day, as well as cultivating a mind of loving-kindness and so forth.

Thinking, "The complete accomplishment of what is desired comes from merit alone," he is devoted to meritorious deeds; thinking, "All accomplishment comes through faith," he increases his faith. (VMv 4.5)
"From vigor comes the completion of what has been undertaken; thus, one should have vigor as the precursor.
From meditative concentration comes stability in the desired fruit; thus, one should have the mind focused solely on meditative concentration. (VMv 4.6)
"Performance [of action] through the renunciation of attachment" means being free from attachment;
"everything belongs to one who possesses right knowledge" means being endowed with knowledge. (VMv 4.7)
Perceiving death as suffering and seeing the nature of life, and being free from all doubt, one should undertake the deception of death. (VMv 4.8)
Therein, first, having recited one hundred thousand mantras of the Enemy of Obstacles (Vighnāri) together with meditation,
one should ward off all obstacles by performing ten thousand fire-oblations (homa).
First, one should utter the words for speech and mind as "Homage to Samantakāya," and thereafter one should speak the words "Homage to the Vajras" and "Homage to Vajrakrodha."
From the word *mahādaṃṣṭrotkaṭapada*, one should utter the word *bhairavāya*;
then [the words] *asimusalaparaśupāśagṛhītahastāya*. (VMv 4.11)

Oṃ, then from the words *amṛtakuṇḍali khakhakhāhi khāhi*, there follow the words *tiṣṭha tiṣṭha*; from that [come] the two words for binding (*bandha*) and the two words for slaying (*hana*). (VMv 4.12)
Then:

"dahadvayaṃ garjadvayaṃ visphoṭayadvayaṃ tataḥ / sarvavajrapadād vighnavināyakān padaṃ vadet //" (VMv 4.13) // Thereafter, one should utter the word "pada" after the words *sarvavajra*, following the two instances of *daha*, the two of *garja*, and the two of *visphoṭaya*.
"From the feet of Mahāgaṇapati, to the one who brings an end to life:
HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ—this is the mantra that wards off obstacles. (VMv 4.14)
Alternatively, one should ward off all obstacles with this very heart-mantra;
through recitation and fire-offerings as before, its power is likewise such.
Oṃ! Having first uttered [the syllables], one then says the words *hulu hulu tiṣṭha tiṣṭha*, followed by *hana hana*, *daha daha*, and likewise again *garja garja*. VMv 4.16.
Expelling all obstacles and obstructors from his body, he should say:
"Oṃ amṛta hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ, perform my protection, svāhā! (VMv 4.17)
Thus, having destroyed all obstacles posed by Māra and being free from agitation,
one should meditate upon the desired yoga for a single day and night.
Performing the deeds of a Buddha, peaceful, dwelling in the Ghanavyūha realm, he sits upon a lotus and moon seat with his vajra-paryaṅka firmly bound. VMv_4.19 //
Having meditated upon white Vairocana, joined with the bodhyagrī mudrā and surrounded by a shimmering circle of white light, one shall not be subject to death as long as saṃsāra endures. VMv_4.20 //

Having meditated upon the Tathāgatas, Akṣobhya and the others, as being richly endowed with their own respective colors, mudrās, and attire, through firm self-identification, one will certainly become a vajra-body.
[One should visualize] the imperishable Lokeśvara, peaceful and resembling the moon, adorned with all ornaments, situated within the cavity of the moon at the heart. VMv 4.22.
He bears the matted locks marked by the perfectly awakened Amitābha of red color,
and he is embraced in the vajra-paryaṅka posture upon his two lotus feet.
With both hands joined in the mudrā of meditative concentration, undisturbed, his body flows with compassion that accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings. VMv 4.24.
Having meditated upon another Lokeśa in his heart as well,
and likewise with a one-pointed mind, [he should place him] again in the heart of that one too.
One should contemplate this meditation for as long as it takes to reach ten million [repetitions];
thereafter, the mind should be directed toward the Lord of the World (Lokanātha), who is subtler than the subtlest.
Upon seeing the Lord of Yoga, death itself indeed dies away;
likewise, the other defects born of the aggregates also come to their own destruction.
Seated upon a moon-disc throne situated in the center of a white lotus,
she sits with her legs bound in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, holding a boon-granting gesture and a blue lotus.
Having the form of the autumn moon's rays, seated upon a moon at her back, fully adorned with all ornaments, and possessing the body of a sixteen-year-old; VMv_4.29.

Having meditated upon Noble Tārā, the mother of all the perfectly awakened ones and their sons, who can assume any form at will, within one’s heart, one should visualize her wheel as having white radiance.

The eight-square grid is filled with eight syllables; the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is placed at the center, beginning with *oṃ* and *hā*, situated within the consonants. (VMv 4.31)
With a one-pointed mind and firm resolve, one should meditate for six months; and with an undistracted mind, one should recite this ten-syllable mantra. (VMv 4.32)
Having first uttered the syllable Oṃ, one should subsequently employ Tāre;
then there should be Tuttāre, followed by Ture, ending with Svāhā—this is the mantra for all rites. (VMv 4.33)
Even by Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, Candra, Arka, Rudra, the guardians of the quarters, and Manmatha,
he conquers death like death itself, with not even a single hair on his body disturbed.
It brings about the destruction of wrinkles, graying hair, misfortune, disease, and poverty;
it is the eradicator of the mass of suffering caused by the eight great fears, such as lions and the like. VMv_4.35 //

The acquisition of food, drink, and so forth without having asked for them; the attainment of palaces, garments, and the like; and the supernatural powers (siddhis) such as the sword, collyrium, foot-ointment, and the auspicious jar. VMv 4.36.
Poetic skill, eloquence, intelligence, and utterly pure wisdom, as well as whatever other desired accomplishment there may be, are produced from this wheel. (VMv 4.37)
Having meditated upon Locanā, Māmakī, Cundā, Mahāśvetā, and the other deities, according to their respective colors, attire, and mudrās, one does not behold death. (VMv 4.38)
Indeed, through union with one's own chosen deity and by being joined with firm ego-identification,
[the self] becomes like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), accomplishing all desired objects.
From that which resembles a conch, a jasmine flower, or the moon, and which abides in the sequence of withdrawal,
death is deceived through the constant practice of its activity.
Having performed the meditation on the form of Heruka as taught in the *Cakrasaṃvara Tantra*, one should,
through its transformation, meditate on the form of a skull-cup.
Whether by contemplating the form of a skeleton or by transforming it into a khaṭvāṅga, death does not approach because [the practitioner] is unfit to be killed. (VMv 4.42)
From the orb of the moon upon his head, he causes drops of nectar to flow,
refreshing every limb through the pores of his skin on all sides.
For six months the yogi, free from all attachments, should practice meditation;
having completely conquered all diseases, he overcomes death as if it were death itself.
Having meditated on a white, thousand-petaled lotus with its face turned downward upon the head, one may destroy death, the beginning of the eon, and so forth, by means of the sequence of moons.

By contemplating this very form of Kṛṣṇa, with its rays that are also of the form of Kṛṣṇa, as it completely drenches [the body], there occurs the destruction of grey hair and other such signs of aging.

Having placed the tongue against the palate and not allowing the teeth to touch the teeth, one should undertake this practice, which is to be believed in due to the power of its inconceivable cause. (VMv 4.47)
One should lick with the tip of the tongue the saliva-laden tongue that is attached above the opening of the throat and facing downward, until the sensation of the nectar-essence is experienced.
Then one shall immediately conquer death and destroy graying hair and other such signs;
by performing that rite, there shall be protection from all calamities and fears.
Alternatively, one may begin another method of mindfulness of breathing;
by increasing the count, one will then certainly attain freedom from old age and death. (VMv 4.50)
Twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths are proclaimed to be the number of breaths for sentient beings in one day and night.
The inhalation of air is praised because it is a collection of nectar;
nectar is the means of life, and by it, death does not afflict one. (VMv 4.52)
One should count the entry of the breath slowly, by numbers such as one hundred thousand;
with a one-pointed mind and according to the rule, this is called silent recitation (*japa*). (VMv 4.53)
By means of this ritual, characterized by silent recitation (japa) and fully perfected,
even a man whose life has been exhausted will certainly live for five more years.
In this way, an increase in lifespan should be inferred from recitations of two hundred thousand or more;
having become skilled in means, one should be devoted to the recitation of the wind-mantra.
If one constantly recites this one thousand times upon rising in the morning,
one will be liberated from all diseases and live as long as the moon and sun endure.
One who lacks practice should not remain [in this state] even for a moment, nor should one sleep;
having conquered sleep through effort, one should [regulate] food, drink, posture, and so forth. (VMv 4.57)
One intent on the movement of the breath should cause it to flow in the natural direction;
the yogi devoted to the natural flow certainly conquers death. (VMv 4.58)
But fools who are solely intent on enjoyments die in the reverse order;
the natural order is direct, while the reverse occurs from its opposite. (VMv 4.59)
Through the binding of the lion’s play mudrā, by the restraint of the vital winds,
or through mastery of the yoga of kumbhaka, cessation occurs which deceives death.
Having slowly filled [the body] with air down to the soles of the feet, retention through suppression constitutes *kumbhaka*; that is called the procedure for recitation (*japa*).
Through the practice of the three types of *udghāta*, *kumbhaka* is mastered;
*udghāta* is considered to be of three kinds according to the divisions of inferior, middling, and so forth. (VMv 4.62)
"Udghāta" is this technical term which indicates the meaning to be explained hereafter:
the deficient [udghāta] consists of thirty-six mātrās, while the middling one is twice that. (VMv 4.63)
The superior [kumbhaka] should be known as threefold; by it, the kumbhaka is mastered.
Having first performed the kumbhaka, one should afterwards [place the hands] upon one's own kneecaps.
Having touched [the tongue] three times with the hand, one should then snap the fingers six times;
this is called a "mātrā" by the learned for the purpose of measuring time.
As long as there are thirty-six *mātrās*, that which constitutes the practice of breath-retention (*kumbhaka*) is considered a "low" *udghāta*; the "middling" is twice that length. (VMv 4.66)
The triple-constituted *udghāta* is the eldest, measuring one hundred and eight *mātrās*;
that very one should be mastered with effort by one who desires to deceive death.
If the retention of breath (kumbhaka) proceeds until the limit of the maximum exhalation, then even the continuous cessation [of breath] becomes well-stabilized. (VMv 4.68)
Having known the day on which one must die, he who remains in cessation—
death does not approach him for thousands of eons.
From the milking of the cow of space, he [obtains] a collection of the liquid essence of nectar by means of the radiant mandala known as Ghaṭāṅkavāruṇa.
The wind emerging from the tip of the nose should repeatedly take up [the moisture] and sprinkle it upon the young bee of the mind that has settled within the withering lotus of the heart.
One should constantly practice this meditation on the milking of space;
even though death beholds him, it does not see him, for he is like space itself. (VMv 4.72)
Having abandoned the wind, one should instead always practice the reality itself; through reality, death as well as other enemies, the Māras, are conquered. (VMv 4.73)
The complete pacification of all defects, the arising of all virtues, and the desired accomplishments of men are won through reality. VMv 4.74.
And that reality is declared to be emptiness, whose nature consists of the excellence of all aspects;
for one who constantly practices that very [emptiness], death comes to be deceived. (VMv 4.75)

The Victors have taught that emptiness is inseparable from the enjoyment body, the dharma body, and so forth, as well as from generosity, ethical discipline, and the rest; it is conjoined with all objects of focus yet free from all objects of focus, and is endowed with the excellence of all aspects. (VM 4.76)
One should not contemplate the conceivable, nor should one contemplate the inconceivable;
one should not contemplate that which is both conceivable and inconceivable; from that, one will attain emptiness.
The wise one should not cultivate existence, nor should he cultivate non-existence;
freed from both existence and non-existence, he should cultivate that which is devoid of them.
One should constantly meditate on emptiness, which is endowed with the excellence of all aspects and free from the grasping of emptiness; by doing so, one is never seen by death.
He does not perceive death, which arises from mere conceptual construction;
nor does he perceive other numerous Māras, nor even saṃsāra.
Thus it is said:
"This so-called death is a conceptual construction [arising] in the absence of all things;
it is slain by one's own conceptualization through the manifestations of ordinary beings. (VMv 4.81)
Conceptual construction is all suffering; conceptual construction is said to be death.
Therefore, one should abandon conceptual construction and become one whose mind is free from conceptual construction.
Whatever is repeatedly meditated upon, distinguished by such qualities as earnestness and so forth,
that very thing attains clarity, just like the mental images of desire, grief, and the like.
For scriptures are indeed easy to find, but their practical applications are very difficult to obtain;
yet in a world where there are those who know the applications, the applications themselves are not difficult to find at all.
Skilled in application, endowed with faith, established in patience and vigor, devoted to practice, and wise—the such person is a vessel for deceiving death. (VMv 4.85)
From physical exertion, such as digestion and drinking, the digestive fire is kindled;
and for one whose fire is thus inflamed, even the transformation of food occurs according to their capacity. (VMv 4.86)
From the transformation [of food] comes the nourishment of the body; from nourishment, the increase of strength;
from strength, the growth of lifespan; and from that growth, long life. (VMv 4.87)

Just as there is no doubt for anyone regarding that which is established by direct perception, so too there is no doubt concerning the lifespan of a kalpa and beyond, because it has been taught [by the Buddha]. (VMv 4.88)
Even when on the verge of extinction, a lamp or similar object persists until the end of an eon through the replenishment of oil and so forth, despite the exhaustion of its oil and wick.
Just so, why should this body, though dying through old age and other afflictions,
not remain until the end of the eon by obtaining the instructions of the perfected ones?
Just as an old house remains standing for a long time through repair, why should it not be so with an old body through its own cultivation? (VMv 4.91)
Nothing is difficult with persistent effort; therefore, strive without laying down the burden.
Even a stream of water, though soft, gradually cleaves through a slab of stone when it flows continuously over time. (VMv 4.92)
Fire is born from wood when it is rubbed; the earth gives water when it is dug.
For men who possess perseverance, nothing is unattainable; all efforts undertaken with justice bear fruit. (VMv 4.93)
Though we have recognized many deceptions regarding death in this world, because we failed to practice [the remedy], we have died smeared with excrement upon our beds. (VMv 4.94)
Those who were skilled in practice, wise, and masters of the treatises, died after extracting their own teeth due to the fault of failing to carry out [the instructions]. VMv 4.95.
Even though they have understood the treatises on yoga and their various applications many times over, they die while preoccupied with the thought, "I shall practice today or tomorrow. (VMv 4.96)
"This I shall do tomorrow, and this again, and this after that"—thus one reflects in vain, placing false hope in the fickle course of worldly existence.
Without having reached the end of its task, a living being—having fallen into the whirlpools of the waters of sense-objects—enters the mouth of death like a ship entering the jaws of a sea-monster.
Thus has been described this deception of the enemy Death, which is to be accomplished through the practice of meditation established by one's own and others' systems;
it must be diligently prepared out of fear of a pitiless death, for in this world there is nothing more desirable than life. (VMv 4.98)
The Vajraḍāka, the Catuṣpīṭha, the Buddhapañjaraka and others, as well as the Kālottara, the Kālāvalī, and the Kālapañcāśikā; VMv 4.99.
Having diligently studied the Jīvapañcāśikā and other such treatises, this "Deception of Death" has been proclaimed out of compassion for sentient beings. (VMv 4.100)
The autumn moon and the sky are utterly pure, yet even with the moon in the clear firmament, they are not fully perfected;
therefore, by whatever merit has been attained that leads to immortality, may all people be liberated from death. (VMv 4.101)
To alleviate the exhaustion of counting, the measure of the text for these ascetic scribes is stated to be three hundred and eighty [verses].
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Instruction on Deceiving Death*, composed by the venerable Paṇḍita Ācārya Vāgīśvarakīrti.
